enrichment.short_title: PI appeal on future earnings and DIY damages
key_facts: Motorcycle courier suffered serious left wrist fractures in a 50/50 liability road accident while working as a courier.
At county court assessment, agreed general damages were £20,000 but four heads of future loss remained in dispute.
The district judge awarded £41,871.43 for future loss of earnings using a multiplier/multiplicand approach based on short pre-accident employment with Kuehne & Nagel.

The Court of Appeal held the evidence was too unreliable for that approach and substituted a round sum of £12,500, reduced the DIY award multiplier, and set aside the loss of congenial employment award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendants' appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court damages assessment following a split-liability personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: future loss of earnings and DIY awards reduced and loss of congenial employment award set aside; increased automatic car costs award upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant has not put before the court reliable evidence of pre- and post-accident earning capacity, a multiplier/multiplicand calculation for future loss of earnings is inappropriate and a round sum should be awarded instead; loss of congenial employment must relate to employment satisfaction, not general loss of amenity from hobbies or social life.
legal_issues: Whether future loss of earnings could be assessed by multiplier/multiplicand on inadequate evidence
Appropriate multiplier for DIY/handyman loss
Whether loss of congenial employment was properly awarded
Whether recurring costs of automatic transmission vehicles were recoverable

enrichment.short_title: Extradition review where fitness to plead disputed

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991

key_facts: Andrew Warren, a UK solicitor, faced extradition to New York on serious securities and fraud charges.
UK psychiatrists concluded he was unfit to plead and that extradition would worsen his mental health and suicidal risk.
The Secretary of State ordered surrender after concluding genuine issues existed as to fitness to stand trial for determination by the New York courts.
Warren sought judicial review of the November 2002 surrender decision on grounds it would be wrong, unjust or oppressive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision under paragraph 8(2) of Schedule 1 to the Extradition Act 1989 to order surrender to the United States.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Secretary of State's decision to order extradition was held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Fitness to stand trial is a matter for the requesting state's courts, not the executive; where medical evidence discloses genuine issues as to fitness and fair procedures exist in the requesting state, the Secretary of State may lawfully order return even where UK psychiatrists consider the accused currently unfit, provided the decision strikes a fair Article 8 balance.
legal_issues: Whether it was wrong, unjust or oppressive to extradite given unanimous UK psychiatric evidence of unfitness
Weight to be given to reports of Mr Bodek appointed by the New York court
Whether genuine issues as to fitness to stand trial existed
Article 8 proportionality of extradition affecting family welfare

enrichment.short_title: Libel case management after defence abandonment
key_facts: Rashid Ghannouchi, leader of the Tunisian Islamist movement An Nahda, sued over an Al Arab article linking him to Al Qaeda and terrorism.
Defendants abandoned justification and qualified privilege on the eve of a strike-out hearing but sought to substitute a damages mitigation plea relying on background context.
The claimant amended particulars to remove characterisation of An Nahda as moderate and democratic.
Gray J refused permission to advance the substituted plea and cross-examination on alleged violent past conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in libel proceedings for case management directions on substituted defence and admissible cross-examination after abandonment of substantive defences.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; defendants not permitted to rely on revised paragraph 11 or proposed cross-examination topics as directly relevant background context.
enrichment.ratio: After abandonment of justification and qualified privilege, a defendant cannot reintroduce effectively a modified justification case under the guise of Burstein background context; stale historical speeches and unverified allegations are not directly relevant background context and would be disproportionate and unfair.
legal_issues: Admissibility of background context under Burstein v Times Newspapers Ltd after strike-out of justification
Whether proposed cross-examination topics amounted to impermissible partial justification
Application of Scott v Sampson and Prager v Times Newspapers Ltd
Case management powers under CPR Part 3

confidence.notes: Clear interlocutory ruling on well-established defamation procedure principles.

enrichment.short_title: Bar Council libel and qualified privilege
key_facts: The Bar Council circulated a letter stating Kearns Agency Limited was not a firm of solicitors and warning barristers not to accept its instructions.
The claimants were in fact solicitors; an apology and correction were sent the next day.
Eady J granted summary judgment for Mark Stobbs on qualified privilege; the claimants appealed.
The circular was sent to all heads of chambers following a barrister's complaint about Kearns' instruction practices.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from summary judgment under CPR Part 24.2 on qualified privilege in libel proceedings against the Bar Council's head of professional standards.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; qualified privilege held to attach to the Bar Council's circular.
enrichment.ratio: In communications within an established relationship such as that between the Bar Council and members of the Bar, qualified privilege attaches where the communication is relevant to their reciprocal duties and interests without requiring prior verification; verification is relevant to malice, not to whether privilege attaches, and Reynolds privilege does not apply to non-media publications.
legal_issues: When verification is relevant to whether qualified privilege attaches
Whether Bar Council communications to members attract common interest qualified privilege
Distinction between Reynolds media privilege and conventional qualified privilege
Whether publication to over 10,000 barristers affects the privilege analysis

confidence.notes: Leading Court of Appeal analysis on verification and qualified privilege in professional body communications.

enrichment.short_title: Lawful development certificate and material operations
key_facts: Imperial Resources sought a lawful development certificate that roof works in November 1988 had commenced implementation of 1983 outline permission for four flats at Leonard Court, Kensington.
Works comprised brick walls around a roof lightwell but lacked window openings and resembled finished parapet walls rather than partial flat construction.
A first inspector's decision was quashed by Ouseley J for focusing only on plan differences; a second inspector dismissed the appeal after a fuller analysis.
The claimant challenged the second decision under section 288.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to a planning inspector's dismissal of an appeal against non-determination of a lawful development certificate application.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the second inspector's decision was upheld as lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Whether material operations are comprised in permitted development requires an objective assessment of the works as a whole, considering significance of differences from approved plans and usability for the permitted scheme; works built as apparently complete parapet walls may not commence development even if on approved alignments.
legal_issues: Whether 1988 wall construction amounted to material operations under section 56
Whether operations were comprised in the 1983 planning permission
Proper approach after Ouseley J's guidance on comparing works with approved plans
Whether inspector erred in treating walls as finished parapets rather than partial construction

linked_authorities.name: Riordan Communications Ltd v South Bucks District Council
Malvern Hills District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Detailed planning judgment applying Ouseley J's earlier guidance with clear fact-specific reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Proof of disqualification in driving while disqualified

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Two consolidated appeals concerned convictions for driving while disqualified under section 103(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act 1988.
In each case magistrates relied on computer court records showing a prior disqualification without formal prosecution evidence.
The prosecution had not adduced a section 73 certificate or other admissible proof that the defendant was the disqualified person.
The DPP conceded both convictions should be quashed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' courts to the High Court on proof of prior disqualification as an ingredient of driving while disqualified.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed and cases remitted with directions to acquit.
enrichment.ratio: The prosecution must prove every ingredient of driving while disqualified including prior disqualification by admissible evidence, typically a section 73 certificate plus proof of identity; magistrates cannot supply missing evidence from their own records or treat matching personal details as sufficient identification.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates may take judicial notice of their own prior disqualification decisions
Proper mode of proof under section 73 of PACE 1984
Whether matching name, date of birth and address suffices to identify the defendant
Admissibility of unsworn computer record information from the court clerk

linked_authorities.name: R v Derwentside Magistrates' Court, ex parte Heaviside
R v Derwentside Justices, ex parte Swift
R v Sunderland Justices, ex parte Bate

confidence.notes: Clear procedural ruling on statutory proof requirements with uncontested outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Challenge to tree preservation order validity
key_facts: Brennon challenged Bromsgrove District Council's confirmation of Tree Preservation Order No 2 of 2002 over trees at 16 Rock Hill during a long-running dispute.
An earlier urgent area-based TPO was replaced after the claimant withdrew a prior section 288 challenge.
The claimant made no representations within the statutory period and later sought out-of-time representations to a fresh committee.
Criminal proceedings for alleged TPO breaches and a planning appeal were pending alongside this challenge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to confirmation of a tree preservation order, including Convention rights arguments.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the TPO was held validly made and confirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Technical compliance with the Trees Regulations 1999 does not require reservice of an unmodified confirmed order; brief amenity reasons and map identification sufficient where trees are clearly identifiable; TPO scheme with consent and appeal rights strikes a fair Article 1 Protocol 1 balance and section 288 review satisfies Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 6 required service of schedule and map after confirmation without modification
Adequacy of reasons under Regulation 3(2)(a)
Accuracy of tree identification on the order map
Whether making the second TPO was an abuse of power or irrational
Compatibility with Articles 6, 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1

enrichment.short_title: Marine insurance costs and CPR Part 36
key_facts: Claimants recovered US$3 million for constructive total loss of the vessel Kastor Too by fire but failed on their primary actual total loss claim.
Each side incurred costs of about £850,000 in a four-week trial.
Claimants made a Part 36 offer of US$2.8 million shortly before trial and beat it at judgment.
Tomlinson J ordered defendants to pay 15% of claimants' costs and claimants to pay 85% of defendants' costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment argument on costs and enhanced interest following successful marine insurance claim for constructive total loss.
enrichment.outcome: Issue-based costs order made; net effect approximately claimants paying 70% of defendants' costs despite beating Part 36 offer.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 36.21 'his costs' refers to costs otherwise awardable under CPR 44.3 and does not override issue-based costs where the successful claimant pursued a distinct issue that substantially increased costs on which it failed; Part 36 does not entitle a claimant to all post-offer costs on an indemnity basis where issue-by-issue analysis would produce a different just result.
legal_issues: Interaction between CPR 36.21 and issue-based costs under CPR 44.3
Whether claimants' actual total loss claim significantly increased trial length and cost
Construction of 'his costs' in CPR 36.21(3)(a)
Appropriate proportionate costs order where claimant succeeds on alternative CTL claim

linked_authorities.name: Johnsey Estates Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions

confidence.notes: Detailed costs judgment analysing novel CPR 36 and issue-costs interaction with clear quantified outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Shared residence order despite Scotland relocation
key_facts: Separated Navy officer and mother of two young girls applied for cross residence orders after traumatic separation including unfounded abuse allegations.
The mother proposed relocating from Hampshire to Edinburgh; the father had resigned his commission before trial.
The children and family reporter recommended sole residence to the mother with generous contact.
The judge made a shared residence order permitting relocation with flexible contact including make-up holiday time if the father remained in England.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court shared residence order with provision for possible relocation to Scotland.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; shared residence order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A shared residence order may reflect substantial time with each parent even where homes are hundreds of miles apart; parental distance does not render shared residence unworkable if the children's year divides meaningfully between homes, and the label marks equal status of each parent's home without requiring exact time equality.
legal_issues: Whether adverse findings against the mother required sole residence to the father
Whether shared residence was appropriate where parents would live in separate jurisdictions
Workability of contact arrangements after relocation to Scotland
When a shared rather than sole residence order should be made

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment with detailed fact findings and clear application of shared residence principles.

enrichment.short_title: Disability Living Allowance life award review
key_facts: Edward Smith had life awards of higher-rate mobility and lowest-rate care components of DLA for osteoarthritis from 1994.
A 1999 medical examination found full pain-free joint movement and that he could walk over 100 metres, prompting review.
The appeal tribunal removed the care component and replaced the mobility life award with a fixed three-year award from March 1999.
Smith continued TV repair work which the tribunal treated as inconsistent with significant care needs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against a Social Security Commissioner's dismissal of appeal from an appeal tribunal reviewing life DLA awards.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal and Commissioner decisions upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where life DLA awards are expressly challenged or reasonable grounds exist to believe entitlement should not continue, the tribunal may review them by comparing original and current evidence; a tribunal need not itemise every changed circumstance if its decision as a whole compares past and present needs and applies the statutory tests.
legal_issues: Whether section 32(4) and section 33(6) were properly applied to life awards
Whether the tribunal failed to identify changed circumstances
Effect of steroid treatment masking osteoarthritis symptoms
Whether continued self-employment negated care component entitlement

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of DLA review statutory framework with clear comparison of 1994 and 1999 medical evidence.
